metadata.title: Leveraging Prior Knowledge in the Development of Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Genome Editing
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

candidates.context: • The scientific soundness of leveraging CMC knowledge may depend on the similarities 104 in the molecular structure of a component 7 or product and its manufacturing process 105 (including the facility and equipment operating conditions). 106 7 FDA’s guidance entitled, “Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing” (January 2024) defines component as any material that is essential for the intended genomic modification, including those that may not appear in the final drug product. GE components may include, but are not limited to, the editor, DNA targeting elements (i.e., elements used to dictate the target DNA sequence, such as guide RNA) and a donor DNA template (i.e., DNA sequence provided to repair the target sequence), if applicable.

candidates.statement: Note, the recommendations provided in this document are not exhaustive. It may be possible to 129 leverage additional types of prior knowledge. Sponsors should submit any leveraging proposals 130 to FDA for consideration, and, if desired, discussion (see section IV). Furthermore, it may be 131 possible to leverage additional knowledge throughout the product lifecycle as product specific 132 experience and knowledge in the field is gained. However, in all cases, when leveraging any 133 kind of prior knowledge, a sponsor should provide a justification for the applicability of the data 134 being leveraged. 135

candidates.statement: Multiple types of CMC knowledge may be considered for potential leveraging 152 throughout a product’s lifecycle. This includes analytical methods, method validation, lot 153 release specifications, stability data, comparability data, and process development and 154 process validation data. The scientific soundness of leveraging prior knowledge will 155 depend on multiple factors. For example, it may depend on the similarities in molecular 156 structure of a product or genome editing component 10 , similar cell source (for ex-vivo 157 modified products), formulation, its manufacturing process (including the facility and 158 equipment operating conditions) and intended therapeutic mechanism. If differences 159 exist, an assessment should be performed to determine if these differences may preclude 160 the use of all or part of the prior knowledge in a given instance, and consider the degree 161 of differences and the level of potential impact on product safety and efficacy. 162

candidates.statement: The scope of nonclinical data needed to support investigational GE products is dependent 385 on the properties, components, and benefit-risk determination for each product. 386 Therefore, a stepwise approach to the nonclinical testing program is recommended where 387 existing knowledge regarding the product and proposed indication should inform the 388 nonclinical program, including kind, duration, and scope of nonclinical testing needed to 389 enter into a clinical trial. The nonclinical program for a product may include leveraging 390 of data to support the rationale and safety for the administration of the investigational 391 product in the proposed clinical trial, as appropriate. Examples of leveraged data that 392 may be considered include the following: a) in vitro studies b) in silico studies, c) other 393 new approach methodologies (NAMs), d) in vivo studies using an analogous animal 394 product, and e) nonclinical data from studies evaluating a relevant product for another 395 indication. The sponsor should integrate data from all available sources to establish 396 adequate scientific justification and safety to support initiation of the proposed clinical 397 trial. DART: For certain GE products, standard DART studies outlined 511 in ICH S5(R3) may not be appropriate given potential differences 512 in product pharmacokinetic profiles, biological activity, and 513 limited relevance of nonclinical animal models. A risk-based 514 approach that evaluates target tissue expression in reproductive 515 organs and BD patterns should be considered when leveraging 516 DART data. Early engagement with the FDA on DART 517 requirements and leveraging data is recommended to avoid 518 unnecessary delays in product development. 519

candidates.statement: iii. Transgene: Even with an identical vector backbone and expression 552 cassette, fundamental differences in transgene expression and 553 functionality can make it challenging to leverage biological 554 activity and safety data between different transgenes. Each 555 transgene may have a unique expression pattern and safety profile 556 depending on transgene-specific properties. Codon optimization 557 strategies may result in distinct expression and toxicity profiles in 558 both on-target and off-target tissues. Furthermore, any integrated 559 selection markers, purification tags, or reporter genes fused to the 560 original transgene may potentially impact the new transgene's 561 intended function. These factors should be addressed when 562 leveraging data and developing the nonclinical program. 563

candidates.statement: i In some cases, clinical data may be available from relevant 567 products that can help to inform certain safety risks and dose level 568 selection for the proposed clinical trial. If existing clinical data is 569 used to help support safety and dose level selection, a discussion 570 should be provided on: a) the similarities and differences between 571 the intended product and the other relevant products demonstrating 572 sufficient similarity, b) ROA, and c) dose levels and dosing 573 regimen evaluated in the previous clinical studies compared to the 574 proposed clinical trial. 575

Sponsors are encouraged to engage in 583 early dialogue with FDA to discuss the appropriateness of 584 leveraging this existing data for their nonclinical development 585 program. 586

candidates.statement: i. The NGS data acquired from genome edited samples can be 636 assessed using a specific set of bioinformatics tools or pipeline(s). 637 A bioinformatics pipeline may include several bioinformatics tools 638 that are implemented in a specific order. For example, NGS data 639 generated from a specific off-target assay may be analyzed using a 640 bioinformatics pipeline specifically developed to analyze such 641 data. Bioinformatics pipelines may be considered for leveraging to 642 analyze similar data obtained from different GE products that were 643 assessed with the same off-target assay. However, specific 644 parameters such as target sequence and mismatch parameters (if 645 applicable) may need to be modified when applying such pipelines 646 to analyze NGS data obtained from different drug products. For 647 example, a GUIDE-seq analysis pipeline implemented for two GE 648 products will differ in the input target sequence if the drug 649 products target distinct regions in the genome. 650
candidates.context: c. Analysis methods and pipelines 634 ii. In lieu of using bioinformatics pipeline(s), sponsors may use a 652 specific tool to perform a specific step of NGS data analysis. 653 Some of these bioinformatics tools may have general utility in 654 analyzing NGS data from different sources (e.g., DNA sequence, 655 RNA sequence, etc.). For example, bioinformatics tools for either 656 sequence quality assessment, or sequence trimming, or sequence 657 alignment have broad utility and may be considered for leveraging 658 to analyze different types of NGS data obtained from testing 659 different GE drug products. 660
